raw_evidence.label: Origin: Moore's 1965 Electronics article
raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law began as a four-page trade-magazine article — not a law of physics. In April 1965, Gordon Moore, then Director of R&D at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote 'Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits' for the journal Electronics. With only five years of integrated-circuit data in hand (1959-1965), he plotted component count against time on a log axis, drew a straight line, and projected that 'by 1975 economics may dictate squeezing as many as 65,000 components on a single silicon chip.' At the time he claimed a doubling roughly every 12 months. The term 'Moore's Law' itself was not coined until around 1970, when Caltech professor Carver Mead started using it. In 1975 Moore revised the rate to a doubling every two years — that is the version that has stuck.

raw_evidence.content: A doubling every two years is a compound annual growth rate of 2^(1/2) - 1 = 0.4142, i.e. 41.4%. For Moore's later 18-month-doubling variant (popularised by Intel's David House) the implied CAGR is 2^(1/1.5) - 1 = 0.5874, i.e. 58.7%. Whichever variant you cite, this is an exponential rate that compounds for decades — and any analysis of the dataset's empirical doubling time should compare the slope of log(transistor_count) vs year against ln(2)/2 ≈ 0.347 per year (two-year doubling) or ln(2)/1.5 ≈ 0.462 (18-month).

raw_evidence.label: Empirical CPU doubling time = 2.03 years (Moore predicted 2.00)
raw_evidence.content: Across the entire 49-year CPU record (1971-2019, n=170), a log-linear fit of transistor count against year gives an empirical doubling time of 2.03 years and a compound annual growth rate of 40.7%. Moore's 1975 revision called for a doubling every 2.00 years (41.4% CAGR). The deviation is 0.03 years over half a century — Gordon Moore's pencil-on-graph-paper extrapolation, drawn in 1965 with only five data points, has held to within 1.5% of its predicted slope across nearly fifty years and seven orders of magnitude of transistor counts. This is the central finding of the dataset.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_01: Empirical doubling time per family ---
print("=== ana_01 ===")
results = []
for fam, df in [('CPU', cpu_c), ('GPU', gpu_c), ('RAM', ram_c)]:
    x = df['date_of_introduction'].values.astype(float)
    y = df['log10_tc'].values
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
    # log10(2) / slope = doubling time in years
    doubling_yr = np.log10(2) / slope
    cagr = (10 ** slope) - 1
    print(f"{fam}: slope_log10/yr={slope:.4f}  doubling={doubling_yr:.2f}yr  CAGR={cagr*100:.1f}%  n={len(df)}  range={int(x.min())}-{int(x.max())}")
    results.append({"family": fam, "slope_log10_per_year": slope, "doubling_years": doubling_yr,
                    "cagr_pct": cagr*100, "n": len(df), "year_min": int(x.min()), "year_max": int(x.max())})
raw_evidence.output:
CPU: slope_log10/yr=0.1483  doubling=2.03yr  CAGR=40.7%  n=170  range=1971-2019
GPU: slope_log10/yr=0.1625  doubling=1.85yr  CAGR=45.4%  n=110  range=1982-2019
RAM: slope_log10/yr=0.1930  doubling=1.56yr  CAGR=56.0%  n=46  range=1963-2018
Moore's predicted log10/yr slope: 0.1505  (doubling = 2.00 yr, CAGR = 41.4%)

raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law began as a four-page trade-magazine article — not a law of physics. In April 1965, Gordon Moore, then Director of R&D at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote 'Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits' for the journal Electronics. In 1975 Moore revised the rate to a doubling every two years — that is the version that has stuck.

raw_evidence.label: From 2,250 to 32 billion: a 14-million-fold CPU climb
raw_evidence.content: The CPU table opens with the Intel 4004 in 1971 carrying 2,250 transistors, the first commercial microprocessor. raw_evidence.label: Origin: Moore's 1965 Electronics article
raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law began as a four-page trade-magazine article — not a law of physics. In April 1965, Gordon Moore, then Director of R&D at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote 'Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits' for the journal Electronics. raw_evidence.label: Origin: Moore's 1965 Electronics article
raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law began as a four-page trade-magazine article — not a law of physics. In April 1965, Gordon Moore, then Director of R&D at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote 'Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits' for the journal Electronics. With only five years of integrated-circuit data in hand (1959-1965), he plotted component count against time on a log axis, drew a straight line, and projected that 'by 1975 economics may dictate squeezing as many as 65,000 components on a single silicon chip.' At the time he claimed a doubling roughly every 12 months. The term 'Moore's Law' itself was not coined until around 1970, when Caltech professor Carver Mead started using it. In 1975 Moore revised the rate to a doubling every two years — that is the version that has stuck.

raw_evidence.content: A doubling every two years is a compound annual growth rate of 2^(1/2) - 1 = 0.4142, i.e. 41.4%. For Moore's later 18-month-doubling variant (popularised by Intel's David House) the implied CAGR is 2^(1/1.5) - 1 = 0.5874, i.e. 58.7%. Whichever variant you cite, this is an exponential rate that compounds for decades — and any analysis of the dataset's empirical doubling time should compare the slope of log(transistor_count) vs year against ln(2)/2 ≈ 0.347 per year (two-year doubling) or ln(2)/1.5 ≈ 0.462 (18-month).

raw_evidence.label: All 326 chips on one chart
raw_evidence.content: Plotting every named chip in the dataset (n=326 with non-null transistor counts and names) on a single log-scale scatter — year on x, transistor count on y, colour by family — produces the canonical Moore's-Law curve. Each row is a discrete data point: a 1971 Intel 4004 at 2,300, a 2019 AMD EPYC Rome at 32 billion, and ~324 chips in between. Hover any point to see the chip's name, year, family, and transistor count. This is the chart Moore drew in 1965 with five points; the dataset has nearly seventy times more.

raw_evidence.content: A doubling every two years is a compound annual growth rate of 2^(1/2) - 1 = 0.4142, i.e. 41.4%. For Moore's later 18-month-doubling variant (popularised by Intel's David House) the implied CAGR is 2^(1/1.5) - 1 = 0.5874, i.e. 58.7%. Whichever variant you cite, this is an exponential rate that compounds for decades — and any analysis of the dataset's empirical doubling time should compare the slope of log(transistor_count) vs year against ln(2)/2 ≈ 0.347 per year (two-year doubling) or ln(2)/1.5 ≈ 0.462 (18-month).

raw_evidence.label: Intel 4004: where the microprocessor begins
raw_evidence.content: The first commercial microprocessor — the chip that anchors the left edge of the CPU dataset — is the Intel 4004, released in November 1971. It packed 2,300 transistors at a 10-micron process node, ran at 740 kHz, and was originally built for Busicom's 141-PF printing calculator. The team was led by Federico Faggin, who developed the silicon-gate technology that made it possible, with Ted Hoff (architecture), Stan Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima (logic design). Faggin signed the die with his initials 'F.F.' Half a century on, this same lineage — Intel 4004 in 1971 with 2,300 transistors → AMD EPYC Rome in 2019 with 32 billion in this dataset — represents a roughly 14-million-fold increase. Real-world high-end chips have since pushed past one trillion (Cerebras WSE-3 at 4 trillion in 2024), but those wafer-scale parts are outside the consumer-CPU/GPU/RAM scope of this Wikipedia table.

raw_evidence.content: The Intel 4004 in 1971 packed 2,300 transistors at a 10,000-nm process node, ran at 740 kHz, and was originally built for the Busicom 141-PF calculator. raw_evidence.label: Why the data has three tables (CPU / GPU / RAM)
raw_evidence.content: Wikipedia's 'Transistor count' page splits the canonical history into separate tables by chip role, and TidyTuesday preserved that split. CPUs are general-purpose programmable processors; GPUs are massively-parallel graphics-and-compute processors that took off after the late-1990s and absolutely dominated the post-2010 transistor curve once deep learning created demand for parallel arithmetic; RAM is dense memory whose 'transistor count' is essentially the bit-cell count and is therefore tied directly to capacity rather than to logic complexity. Comparing them on the same axis is fair (they are all etched on the same lithography roadmap) but the three lines tell different stories: CPUs were the early leaders, GPUs caught up in the 2000s and have led the absolute count since the late 2010s, and RAM tracks capacity scaling that is more linear-in-bits-per-die than logic.

raw_evidence.label: Three families, three slopes — RAM doubles fastest at 1.56 years
raw_evidence.content: The three chip families do not march at the same pace. RAM doubles every 1.56 years (56.0% CAGR, 1963-2018), GPUs every 1.85 years (45.4% CAGR, 1982-2019), and CPUs every 2.03 years (40.7% CAGR, 1971-2019). RAM's faster slope reflects that 'transistor count' for memory is essentially the bit-cell count — capacity scales near-linearly with cells, so doubling capacity directly doubles transistors. CPUs spend their transistor budget on logic complexity, which has historically scaled at exactly the rate Moore drew on his graph. GPUs sit in between, accelerating after 2005 once parallel arithmetic became the default tool for both graphics and machine learning.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_01: Empirical doubling time per family ---
print("=== ana_01 ===")
results = []
for fam, df in [('CPU', cpu_c), ('GPU', gpu_c), ('RAM', ram_c)]:
    x = df['date_of_introduction'].values.astype(float)
    y = df['log10_tc'].values
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
    # log10(2) / slope = doubling time in years
    doubling_yr = np.log10(2) / slope
    cagr = (10 ** slope) - 1
    print(f"{fam}: slope_log10/yr={slope:.4f}  doubling={doubling_yr:.2f}yr  CAGR={cagr*100:.1f}%  n={len(df)}  range={int(x.min())}-{int(x.max())}")
    results.append({"family": fam, "slope_log10_per_year": slope, "doubling_years": doubling_yr,
                    "cagr_pct": cagr*100, "n": len(df), "year_min": int(x.min()), "year_max": int(x.max())})

Source: 1965: Moore's Law Predicts the Future of Integrated Circuits — Computer History Museum (https://www.computerhistory.org/siliconengine/moores-law-predicts-the-future-of-) Facts: Moore was Director of R&D at Fairchild Semiconductor when he published the 1965 article; He projected ~65,000 components on a single chip by 1975 Source: Gordon Moore (1965) — Cramming more components onto integrated circuits, Electronics, vol. 38 no. 8, April 19, 1965 (https://hasler.ece.gatech.edu/Published_papers/Technology_overview/gordon_moore_) Facts: The article was published in Electronics magazine, Volume 38, Number 8, April 19, 1965

raw_evidence.label: Origin: Moore's 1965 Electronics article
raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law began as a four-page trade-magazine article — not a law of physics. In April 1965, Gordon Moore, then Director of R&D at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote 'Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits' for the journal Electronics. With only five years of integrated-circuit data in hand (1959-1965), he plotted component count against time on a log axis, drew a straight line, and projected that 'by 1975 economics may dictate squeezing as many as 65,000 components on a single silicon chip.' At the time he claimed a doubling roughly every 12 months. The term 'Moore's Law' itself was not coined until around 1970, when Caltech professor Carver Mead started using it. In 1975 Moore revised the rate to a doubling every two years — that is the version that has stuck.

raw_evidence.label: How close did Moore's 1965 prediction land?
raw_evidence.content: Moore's 1965 paper said that 'by 1975 economics may dictate squeezing as many as 65,000 components on a single silicon chip'. Looking at the CPUs actually shipping in 1974-1976 in this dataset, the highest count is 8,500 (Zilog Z80, 1976); 1975 itself topped out at 5,000 transistors. Moore's prediction overshot by roughly an order of magnitude — the kind of error any forecaster makes when extrapolating an exponential. He partly self-corrected in 1975 by halving the doubling rate from 12 months to 24, which is the slope that subsequently held for half a century. The 1965 paper was directionally right and quantitatively early; the 1975 revision is the version that aged into a law.

print(f"\nActual CPUs released 1974-1976:")
print(near[['processor', 'date_of_introduction', 'transistor_count']].to_string(index=False))
# Closest single chip near 65K in 1975 era
# Extrapolate from fit
x_eval = np.array([1975.0])
y_eval = cs * x_eval + ci
pred_from_fit = 10 ** y_eval

# Highest 1975 actual
cpu_1975 = cpu_c[cpu_c['date_of_introduction']==1975]['transistor_count'].max() if (cpu_c['date_of_introduction']==1975).any() else None
print(f"highest 1975 actual: {cpu_1975}")

# --- ana_15: First chip past 1 million / 1 billion transistors ---
print("=== ana_15 ===")
all_c = pd.concat([cpu_c.assign(family='CPU', name=cpu_c['processor']),
                    gpu_c.assign(family='GPU', name=gpu_c['processor'])], ignore_index=True)
all_c = all_c.sort_values('date_of_introduction')
thresholds = [1e3, 1e4, 1e5, 1e6, 1e7, 1e8, 1e9, 1e10]
for thr in thresholds:
    hit = all_c[all_c['transistor_count'] >= thr]
    if len(hit) > 0:
        first = hit.sort_values('date_of_introduction').iloc[0]
        print(f"  first to reach {thr:>12,.0f} transistors: {int(first['date_of_introduction'])} {first['family']} {first['name']}  ({int(first['transistor_count']):,})")

raw_evidence.label: Origin: Moore's 1965 Electronics article
raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law began as a four-page trade-magazine article — not a law of physics. In April 1965, Gordon Moore, then Director of R&D at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote 'Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits' for the journal Electronics. With only five years of integrated-circuit data in hand (1959-1965), he plotted component count against time on a log axis, drew a straight line, and projected that 'by 1975 economics may dictate squeezing as many as 65,000 components on a single silicon chip.' At the time he claimed a doubling roughly every 12 months. The term 'Moore's Law' itself was not coined until around 1970, when Caltech professor Carver Mead started using it. In 1975 Moore revised the rate to a doubling every two years — that is the version that has stuck.

Looking at the CPUs actually shipping in 1974-1976 in this dataset, the highest count is 8,500 (Zilog Z80, 1976); 1975 itself topped out at 5,000 transistors. Moore's prediction overshot by roughly an order of magnitude — the kind of error any forecaster makes when extrapolating an exponential. sentences.summary: det_03: Intel 4004: where the microprocessor begins. Source: Intel 4004 — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel_4004) Facts: Intel 4004 was the first commercial microprocessor available for general use; It contained 2,300 transistors on a single chip

raw_evidence.label: Intel 4004: where the microprocessor begins
raw_evidence.content: The first commercial microprocessor — the chip that anchors the left edge of the CPU dataset — is the Intel 4004, released in November 1971. It packed 2,300 transistors at a 10-micron process node, ran at 740 kHz, and was originally built for Busicom's 141-PF printing calculator. The team was led by Federico Faggin, who developed the silicon-gate technology that made it possible, with Ted Hoff (architecture), Stan Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima (logic design). Faggin signed the die with his initials 'F.F.' Half a century on, this same lineage — Intel 4004 in 1971 with 2,300 transistors → AMD EPYC Rome in 2019 with 32 billion in this dataset — represents a roughly 14-million-fold increase. Real-world high-end chips have since pushed past one trillion (Cerebras WSE-3 at 4 trillion in 2024), but those wafer-scale parts are outside the consumer-CPU/GPU/RAM scope of this Wikipedia table.

raw_evidence.label: Order-of-magnitude milestones: from 1K to 10B transistors
raw_evidence.content: The dataset crosses each power-of-ten milestone roughly every 7 years. The first CPU past 1,000 transistors was the Intel 4004 in 1971; past 10,000 was Intel 8086 in 1978; past 100,000 was Intel 80286 in 1982; past 1 million was Intel i860 in 1989; past 10 million was Hitachi SH-4 in 1997; past 100 million was SPARC64 V in 2001; past 1 billion was the dual-core Itanium 2 in 2006; past 10 billion was the 32-core SPARC M7 in 2015. Seven 10x crossings in 44 years, spaced 4-7 years apart — exactly the rhythm a 2-year doubling produces.

raw_evidence.label: Over- and under-performers: who beat the line, who lagged
raw_evidence.content: Residuals to a per-family log-linear fit reveal two distinct categories of chip. Over-performers — chips that landed higher above the trend than their year predicted — are dominated by Intel's Itanium 2 family (the dual-core Itanium 2 in 2006 sits +0.95 log-units above the line, the largest residual in the CPU record) and SPARC64. Under-performers, sitting below the line, are mostly low-power and embedded designs: ARM 9TDMI (1999, -2.20), ARM 1, ARM 2, ARM Cortex-A9, Intel Atom — chips whose design goals trade transistor count for power efficiency. The same line therefore separates two design philosophies as much as it separates two eras.
raw_evidence.code:
x = df['date_of_introduction'].astype(float).values
    y = np.log10(df['transistor_count'].astype(float).values)
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
    yhat = slope * x + intercept

raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law began as a four-page trade-magazine article — not a law of physics. In April 1965, Gordon Moore, then Director of R&D at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote 'Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits' for the journal Electronics. raw_evidence.label: Moore's prediction line vs actual CPU max — a near-perfect overlay
raw_evidence.content: Drawing Moore's 2-year doubling line through the Intel 4004's 2,300 transistors at 1971 and projecting forward to 2019 gives a predicted ~38.6 billion transistors. Across the 48-year window, the actual CPU max is almost always within a single order of magnitude of the Moore line, oscillating above (Itanium era, 2003-2008) and below (mid-2010s before EPYC Rome) the prediction.

raw_evidence.label: Origin: Moore's 1965 Electronics article
raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law began as a four-page trade-magazine article — not a law of physics. In April 1965, Gordon Moore, then Director of R&D at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote 'Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits' for the journal Electronics. With only five years of integrated-circuit data in hand (1959-1965), he plotted component count against time on a log axis, drew a straight line, and projected that 'by 1975 economics may dictate squeezing as many as 65,000 components on a single silicon chip.' At the time he claimed a doubling roughly every 12 months. The term 'Moore's Law' itself was not coined until around 1970, when Caltech professor Carver Mead started using it. In 1975 Moore revised the rate to a doubling every two years — that is the version that has stuck.

raw_evidence.label: Moore's prediction line vs actual CPU max — a near-perfect overlay

raw_evidence.label: Final ITRS roadmap (2016) — Moore's Law was officially un-mapped
raw_evidence.content: For nearly two decades the industry coordinated transistor scaling through the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS), a global document that effectively codified Moore's Law. In 2016 ITRS released its final roadmap and dissolved. The closing report concluded that traditional 2-D transistor scaling would hit an economic wall by ~2021, after which the industry would have to lean on 3-D stacking, advanced packaging, and specialised accelerators rather than simple lithographic shrink. SIA, a major ITRS sponsor, formally announced the transition. This makes 2016 a useful narrative inflection point — but the dataset cuts off in 2019, so it captures the very first chips of the post-ITRS era (Apple A12X, Nvidia Turing, AMD EPYC Rome) without yet reaching the trillion-transistor wafer-scale chips that arrived afterward.

raw_evidence.label: After the dataset: trillion-transistor wafer-scale chips
raw_evidence.content: The dataset stops at 2019. Anyone reading the blog today will know the curve has continued to accelerate, not slow down — but along radically different vectors. In 2022 Apple's M1 Ultra fused two M1 Max dies via a 2.5-D silicon interposer for 114 billion transistors on a 5 nm node, the most ever in a personal-computer chip. In 2024 Cerebras unveiled the WSE-3 wafer-scale engine: a single piece of silicon with 4 trillion transistors, more than 100 times the count of any chip in the TidyTuesday tables. AMD's MI300A AI accelerator integrated ~150 billion. None of these appear in the dataset, so the analysis must be careful to say 'within the dataset' when describing the maximum and the leader, and to note that the modern frontier is now driven by AI accelerators and chiplet packaging rather than by the classic CPU race the dataset starts with.

raw_evidence.label: GPUs held the absolute lead for 11 separate years — most of them recent
raw_evidence.content: Comparing the per-year maximum transistor count between CPUs and GPUs, GPUs hit the absolute lead in 11 different years between 1998 and 2017. Modern years are increasingly tight: in 2010 the top GPU was 1.15x the top CPU; by 2016 it was 1.91x; in 2018 CPUs took the lead back at 1.27x. Across 2010-2019 the GPU/CPU max ratio hovered between 0.32 and 1.91 — a coexistence rather than a takeover. The CPU stays in front overall (37 of 48 years), but the GPU narrative — that parallel arithmetic eats the world after 2010 — is too clean: in the data, the lead has flipped back and forth.
raw_evidence.code:
recent['gpu_to_cpu_ratio'] = recent['GPU_max'] / recent['CPU_max'].replace(0, np.nan)
print(recent[['CPU_max', 'GPU_max', 'gpu_to_cpu_ratio']].to_string())
raw_evidence.output:
Years GPU max > CPU max: 11
first GPU lead year: 1998
last GPU lead year:  2017
2018: CPU 23.6B  GPU 18.6B  ratio 0.79
2019: CPU 32.0B  GPU 10.3B  ratio 0.32

raw_evidence.content: Comparing the per-year maximum transistor count between CPUs and GPUs, GPUs hit the absolute lead in 11 different years between 1998 and 2017. Modern years are increasingly tight: in 2010 the top GPU was 1.15x the top CPU; by 2016 it was 1.91x; in 2018 CPUs took the lead back at 1.27x. raw_evidence.label: Final ITRS roadmap (2016) — Moore's Law was officially un-mapped
raw_evidence.content: For nearly two decades the industry coordinated transistor scaling through the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS), a global document that effectively codified Moore's Law. In 2016 ITRS released its final roadmap and dissolved. The closing report concluded that traditional 2-D transistor scaling would hit an economic wall by ~2021, after which the industry would have to lean on 3-D stacking, advanced packaging, and specialised accelerators rather than simple lithographic shrink. SIA, a major ITRS sponsor, formally announced the transition. This makes 2016 a useful narrative inflection point — but the dataset cuts off in 2019, so it captures the very first chips of the post-ITRS era (Apple A12X, Nvidia Turing, AMD EPYC Rome) without yet reaching the trillion-transistor wafer-scale chips that arrived afterward.
